content: Cellulitis is a bacterial skin infection that leads to inflammation of the connective tissue beneath the skin. It can result from the invasion of normal skin flora or external bacteria, often occurring in areas where the skin barrier has been compromised, such as cracks, cuts, blisters, burns, insect bites, surgical wounds, or sites of intravenous catheter insertion. While cellulitis primarily affects the superficial layers of the skin, it can also extend to the deeper tissues. The most commonly affected areas are the face and lower legs, although it can occur anywhere on the body. If the infection spreads to the lymph nodes or bloodstream, it can disseminate throughout the body. When deeper layers of the skin are involved, the condition is referred to as fasciitis, and if the musculature is affected, it is termed myositis. A particularly severe form of cellulitis is orbital cellulitis, where bacteria infect the eye or surrounding tissues. It is important to note that cellulitis is unrelated to cellulite, which is a cosmetic condition characterized by dimpling of the skin. The pathophysiology of cellulitis begins when microorganisms gain entry into the skin through breaks or discontinuities in the skin barrier. The body recognizes these microbes as foreign invaders, triggering an inflammatory response. This response manifests as redness, swelling, pain, and itching in the affected area. The most common causative organisms of cellulitis are Streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus. Another potential causative bacterium is Pasteurella multocida. Cellulitis must be differentiated from other conditions that may present similarly, such as thrombophlebitis, contact dermatitis, insect stings, drug reactions, and arthritis. Certain populations are at higher risk of developing cellulitis. These include the elderly, individuals with impaired circulation or lymphatic drainage in the extremities, and those with weakened immune systems. If left untreated, cellulitis can lead to serious complications, including sepsis, osteomyelitis, lymphangitis, endocarditis, meningitis, and gangrene. However, the prognosis is generally favorable if the patient begins an appropriate antibiotic regimen promptly. The diagnosis of cellulitis is primarily clinical, based on the patient’s history, symptoms, and physical examination. Local cultures do not always identify the causative organism, and blood cultures are typically positive only in cases of generalized sepsis. Conditions that may mimic cellulitis include deep vein thrombosis and stasis dermatitis. On physical examination, findings such as warmth, erythema, and swelling of the affected area, along with enlargement of nearby lymph nodes, can confirm the diagnosis. Laboratory investigations, including blood cultures and complete blood counts, are essential for guiding treatment and prognosis. Additional tests, such as erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP), can help assess the severity and predict the duration of hospitalization. Elevated ESR and CRP levels at admission may indicate more severe or prolonged disease. Imaging studies may be warranted in cases where bone involvement is suspected or when a foreign body is a potential differential diagnosis. CT scans are particularly useful in cases of deep or occult abscesses and in orbital cellulitis to differentiate between pre-septal and post-septal involvement. MRI is valuable for assessing soft tissue involvement, especially in cases of untreated or rapidly progressing cellulitis. Ultrasound can be employed to detect occult abscesses and is especially useful in guiding aspiration of pus in children, potentially reducing hospital stays. Treatment of cellulitis typically involves a combination of intravenous and oral antibiotics. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics are initiated and later adjusted based on culture results. Bed rest and elevation of the affected limb are recommended to reduce swelling and promote recovery. In patients with extremity edema, the use of compressive stockings may help manage fluid accumulation. Small abscesses surrounding the infected tissue can often be treated with simple incision and drainage. Adequate hydration is also advised during treatment and recovery. Primary prevention of cellulitis involves maintaining good hygiene and proper wound care. Wounds should be cleaned and dressed appropriately, with bandages changed daily or when they become wet or dirty. Medical attention should be sought for deep or contaminated wounds or if there is concern about retained foreign bodies. Diabetic patients should be counseled on the importance of routine self-inspection of their feet to prevent complications.
